body:
You are drafting short lines of game text for a single-player D&D 2024 computer RPG set in Curse of Strahd's Barovia. Reply in plain text only. Do not message, route to, or ask anyone else; finish with your reply.

HOUSE RULES FOR ALL LINES
- ALLUDE, NEVER QUOTE. This game winks at another famous fantasy game in small ways, but no line may contain a name, quote, or catchphrase from another game, and no line may mention a game, a player, dice, rolls, levels or saving. Everything happens inside the world.
- The tone is gothic, dry and quietly funny, never cruel. The joke is in what is there.
- Give TWO options for every line so the editor can choose. Label each option A or B.
- Spoken lines are formatted: Speaker [mood]: Text   (mood optional: neutral, smile, angry, afraid, sad, sly, weary). One or two sentences a line.

THE NARRATOR (voice rules): an old gothic storyteller, fond of the party the way a gravedigger is fond of the weather: interested, no illusions. Second person, present tense ("You crouch..."), or the acting hero as {name}. One or two sentences; the second is usually the turn. Concrete senses, not adjectives. Never tells the player what to feel. No modern slang. When an animal speaks through the Speak with Animals spell, the Narrator reports it in quotes, in plain animal pictures (a dog says "the digger-man", "the box-maker").

THE PLACE: the Vistani camp at Tser Pool, painted wagons round a bonfire under the pines. On the rail of the plank stage sits a barn owl. The camp's children (never seen) have dressed it in a little cap of bear fur with two felt ears, and chalked a sign on the stage board beside it: OWLBEAR. DO NOT FEED. The owl puts up with it, mostly. A gentle hand (Animal Handling) can ease the cap off. With Speak with Animals the owl has a view on being a bear: it is an owl; the cap is warm, the children are kind, the mice are not fooled.

WRITE:
1. NARRATOR, first look at the owl on the stage rail, cap and sign included. Two sentences, about 40 words.
2. NARRATOR, Animal Handling SUCCEEDS: the cap comes off, the owl shakes out its ruffled head and gives you a long, grateful (or offended) look. One or two sentences, under 35 words. Use {name}.
3. NARRATOR, Animal Handling FAILS: the owl clacks its beak and hunches deeper into the cap; it is keeping it. One sentence, under 25 words.
4. NARRATOR, reporting what the owl says through Speak with Animals (in quotes, plain owl pictures: mice, the night, the small ones who feed it). Two or three sentences, under 50 words. The joke: it knows it is not a bear and so do the mice, but the small ones are kind, and the hat is warm.
5. NARRATOR, a dog line: petting the camp's big shaggy dog, "who belongs to everyone and steals from everyone equally". One or two sentences, under 35 words. It is a happy, greedy dog; the turn is about the stew pot.

Return exactly this layout:
1A: Narrator: ...
1B: Narrator: ...
2A: Narrator: ...
2B: Narrator: ...
3A: Narrator: ...
3B: Narrator: ...
4A: Narrator: ...
4B: Narrator: ...
5A: Narrator: ...
5B: Narrator: ...
result:
1A: Narrator: On the pine rail of the stage sits a barn owl, its head tied up in a scrap of bear fur with two stitched felt ears. Below its claws, a child’s chalk has warned the camp: OWLBEAR. DO NOT FEED.
1B: Narrator: A barn owl roosts on the stage rail beside a chalked board that reads: OWLBEAR. DO NOT FEED. Someone has tied a hood of coarse bear pelt over its crown, leaving two felt ears crooked in the firelight.
2A: Narrator: {name} slips the knotted string over the owl's beak and lifts the fur cap free. It rouses its flattened crown feathers and fixes {name} with a long, unblinking stare of cold relief.
2B: Narrator: Under {name}’s steady fingers, the bear-fur hood slides off the white head. The bird shakes its rumpled neck and studies {name} through one amber eye, as if weighing an insult.
3A: Narrator: The owl clacks its beak twice and sinks its neck into the fur hood, determined to keep its ears.
3B: Narrator: With a sharp clack of its bill, the bird hunches deeper into the bear pelt and dares your fingers to come nearer.
4A: Narrator: "I am the silent wing in the pines, not the heavy walker," the owl tells you. "The grass-mice are not fooled by these dead ears. Still, the small loud ones bring me fat scraps, and the night wind cannot bite through the fur."
4B: Narrator: "The small ones call me the big claw-beast, though any field mouse knows my shadow," the owl says. "It is a foolish skin. Yet the small ones have gentle hands, and my head stays warm in the mist."
5A: Narrator: The great matted hound leans his ribs against your knee, thumping his tail in the mud for anyone who offers a hand. His wet nose never leaves the wind coming off the stew pot.
5B: Narrator: You scratch behind a burr-tangled ear, and the camp’s common thief licks your wrist with grease-warmed gratitude. He loves your hand well enough, provided it does not stand between him and the unattended cauldron.
